newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Buba's Krupp dampens rate rise speculation.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Buba's Krupp dampens rate rise speculation.

text.p: Bundesbank council member Hans-Juergen Krupp on Monday dampened market speculation of an imminent rise in German interest rates, saying such a move now would severely damage the domestic economy.

Conceding the Bundesbank was in a "dilemma," Krupp said a small interest rate rise would probably fail to have a significant impact on currency markets while a larger hike was not justifiable against the backdrop of a weak German economy.

"...there is pressure on the central bank to raise interest rates for currency reasons," Krupp said in the text of a speech. "But an interest rate increase would be highly damaging for domestic economic reasons."

The comments are likely to allay fears that the Bundesbank will raise its main money market rate on Tuesday when it sets its next auction for securities repurchase agreements, or on Thursday when its council meets after a four-week summer break.
Speculation the Bundesbank may raise rates grew in recent weeks as the mark's depreciation accelerated.
Several Bundesbank officials fanned expectations of a hike by saying they were concerned about the mark's fall and were scrutinising signs of an uptick in inflation.

The dollar climbed to an eight-year high of 1.89 marks two weeks ago but has since fallen back about seven pfennigs, prompting economists to predict the Bundesbank will refrain from a rate rise this week.

Krupp, generally regarded as a dove on the Bundesbank's council, agreed that the speed of the mark's decline this year was worrying but noted he saw no imminent inflationary dangers resulting from the mark's fall.
"Such a depreciation can lead to imported inflation. The continued weak economy means that no inflation movement is discernible at the moment," Krupp said.

Given the globalisation of financial markets, individual central banks and nations had limited scope to influence currency markets. Interest rate increases may be the most promising tool, Krupp said, adding:
"But that does not answer the question of how large the interest rate change should be to influence the exchange rate.

"There is much to suggest that a small interest rate rise would have no significant impact on the exchange rate, and a bigger interest rate rise, whose impact would also be uncertain, could not be justified in domestic economic terms.
"At the present Germany is a very good example of the dilemma of central banks."
The recent slight rise in German inflation was caused by changes to the health care system and in car taxation.

German consumer inflation rose to a year-on-year rate of 1.9 percent in July from 1.7 percent in June, with the month-on-month rate rising to 0.5 percent from 0.2 percent following a rise in prescription charges and the introduction of new tax rates for car owners in July.
Since there was a limit to what policymakers could do to influence currency markets, Europe's planned monetary union offered the only chance to end currency turmoil, Krupp said.
The planned single currency, or euro, would remove exchange rates in Europe and probably be less volatile against the dollar and the yen than individual European currencies are now, he said.
He added the European Union had made all necessary institutional preparations to allow the planned single currency to be as stable as the mark.

In view of the success so far of nations' efforts to achieve monetary stability, it was likely that a "sufficient number" of nations would fulfil the inflation, interest rate and exchange rate criteria.

He also reiterated that the Maastricht Treaty on European Union did not require exact adherence to the deficit criterion which states that a country's deficit must not exceed three percent of gross domestic product.
